WHO WE ARE

A creative entertainment company built on old stories and new engineering.

Odin Kin Entertainment is a creative entertainment company dedicated to designing immersive worlds where folklore, horror, mythology, and fantasy come to life.

Through storytelling, engineering, interactive technology, themed attractions, and original intellectual properties, Odin Kin creates experiences that blur the boundary between imagination and reality.

OUR MISSION

To bring legends to life through imagination, craftsmanship, and immersive experiences.

OUR VISION

To become a leading creator of myth-inspired immersive entertainment, blending storytelling, artistry, engineering, and technology to redefine how people experience fantasy and horror.

Guest Reviews

I went to Feather & Fang with three friends and honestly Whisperwood was probably my favorite part of the whole night. The fog, sounds, lighting, and all the little details made it feel like we were actually walking somewhere we weren't supposed to be. There was one creature performer who noticed our group, stopped what they were doing, stared at us, and followed us for a little while before disappearing between the trees. We LOST IT. 😂

That was probably my favorite moment because it felt like it happened specifically to us. For a second I wasn't watching an attraction anymore. I felt like something in Ravenfall had actually noticed us.

I just wish there were more moments like that.

There were some AMAZING-looking creatures and objects along the paths, but sometimes... nothing happened. At one point we found this really creepy creature and all four of us stopped because we were convinced it was going to move. We waited... and waited... and eventually realized it was just part of the scenery. It looked incredible, but imagine if its eyes suddenly opened when you got close, or it moved when you weren't looking, or somehow reacted differently depending on what you did!

The only thing I really hated was when effects became predictable. There was one scare that activated for the group walking ahead of us. We watched it happen, waited, walked forward, and basically knew exactly when it was going to happen to us too. I could tell it was probably just repeating on a timer. After that, it wasn't scary anymore.

I don't necessarily need everything jumping at me. I just want to feel like the things in Ravenfall know I'm there.

If something notices me before I notice it... THAT would be terrifying.

Would I return? Absolutely. Just please make the forest a little less predictable next time. 👀

This was my second visit to Feather & Fang, this time with my 13-year-old daughter. I'm probably not the typical person running around trying to get scared as much as possible. I'm much more interested in creature design, mythology, practical movie effects, and seeing how these environments are made.

From that perspective, Feather & Fang is fantastic.

The creature work was easily my favorite part. I love being able to get close enough to see textures, mechanical details, unusual materials, and little movements that make something feel alive. I'll take a physical creature over a video screen any day. There were a few moments where we weren't even sure whether something was a prop or a performer, which was great.

What surprised me was that the scariest moments weren't necessarily the loud ones. There was an area where we could hear something moving before we could see it. Another creature seemed to move slightly whenever we weren't looking directly at it. Those moments built suspense and gave us time to realize that something wasn't right.

I wish there were more experiences like that—things you slowly discover. Maybe observant guests notice a creature's eyes following them, a sound changes as they get closer, or some strange artifact starts behaving differently when someone approaches. Give us a moment to think, "Wait... did that just move?"

My least favorite experience was basically the opposite. A very loud effect suddenly activated close to my daughter. She was done after that. She refused to enter the next area because she thought another speaker was going to go off next to her.

I know this is a Halloween park. We're expecting to be scared! I'm definitely not asking Feather & Fang to stop being frightening. But there is a difference between building fear and simply being loud.

The best experiences made both of us curious and uncomfortable at the same time. The weakest ones were basically: walk here, loud noise, jump.

Give me a creature slowly realizing I'm standing there instead.

That's much creepier.

Would I return? Yes—and my daughter says yes too, as long as I go first next time.

I've been to Feather & Fang twice now, and the reason I came back was the performers. There are a lot of places where you walk through a haunted attraction and everything happens exactly the same way for every person. Feather & Fang has moments where it actually feels like you're interacting with whatever lives there.

One creature came around a corner, saw our group, and completely changed what it was doing. It tilted its head, backed away, watched us for a second, and then suddenly came toward us. My friends and I spent the next ten minutes arguing about whether it was curious about us or trying to hunt us. 😂

THAT is what I want more of.

I would love to see the costumes themselves become even more expressive. Some of them look incredible, but the faces and hands don't really change. Imagine if a creature's ears moved when it heard you, its eyes changed when it noticed you, its claws moved, or you heard a sound actually coming from the creature instead of somewhere in the room. If the costume reacted along with the performer, I think you'd stop seeing "a person wearing a costume" and start seeing the creature.

There was one thing I absolutely hated, though.

One interactive area had instructions.

There was literally a sign telling us where to stand and what we needed to do to make something happen. People started forming a little line and somebody in front of us said, "You stand there and wave your hand, then it activates."

Well... thanks. Mystery gone. 😂

If I'm supposed to believe I'm exploring Ravenfall, I don't want Ravenfall giving me an instruction manual. Let me discover it! If something responds when I walk closer, touch something, move, make noise, or naturally interact with the environment, that's awesome. Just don't make me stop and figure out how to operate the attraction.

I also noticed one performer constantly adjusting something on their costume. Every time they fixed it, I stopped seeing the creature and started thinking about the person inside wearing a complicated costume. Whatever technology you put on performers has to let them actually perform.

The best Feather & Fang moments make you forget you're at a theme park.

More of that, please.

Would I return? Already planning visit #3. And I am still not reading your haunted instruction signs.
AN ODIN KIN ORIGINAL UNIVERSE

Ravenfall

Long before maps gave names to every forest, mountain, and sea, people told stories about creatures that lived just beyond the firelight. Over centuries those stories became myths, then fairy tales, then entertainment — and people stopped believing. But the creatures never disappeared. They simply learned to hide.

RAVENFALL is near us!?

Something is happening inside Odin Kin.

Huginn Creative team insists they invented Ravenfall.

The Freki Moonforge team insists some of their designs occasionally behave in ways nobody programmed.

And every October, ravens begin gathering on the roof of Feather & Fang entrances.

Probably a coincidence. Probably.

THE BOUNDARY

The Veil

It does not form a wall. It influences what people perceive.

Ravenfall is a hidden realm existing alongside human world — not another planet or a distant fantasy kingdom, but the forgotten spaces: forests people no longer enter, tunnels beneath old cities, abandoned villages, mountain paths erased from maps.

For thousands of years the boundary separating Ravenfall from the human world remained strong. A traveler might walk past the entrance to Ravenfall and see nothing more than trees. Someone might hear a creature moving behind them but convince themselves it was only the wind. The Veil let both worlds exist side by side, each unaware of how close the other really was.

The weakening Veil now creates temporary openings called Rifts — inside an abandoned building, beneath an old bridge, between trees, inside a tunnel, or within an object tied to an old legend. Near a Rift, light changes, electronics malfunction, sounds repeat, temperatures drop. Some Rifts last seconds. Others last years. Lately, they've been appearing more often.

ONE AUTUMN NIGHT

The Sundering

One minute and thirteen seconds that changed everything.

No one knows exactly what caused it. Some believe an ancient artifact was disturbed. Others believe humans simply stopped believing in the old stories, weakening the Veil. Some whisper that something on the other side deliberately opened the way.

Whatever the cause, one autumn night thousands of ravens suddenly appeared across the sky, flying in enormous spirals. Then, all at once, they fell. Not dead — waiting. For exactly one minute and thirteen seconds, every raven remained completely still. Then they rose together and disappeared into the darkness.

That night became known as the Sundering. Afterward, the Veil began to fail.

ravens appear at nearly every documented rift

The Watchers

No one knows whom — or what — they serve.

Researchers initially believed ravens were simply attracted to Rifts. They were wrong. The ravens appear to be observing them. Sometimes they warn people of approaching danger. Sometimes they guide travelers toward hidden locations. Sometimes they steal objects and carry them through the Veil.

Within Ravenfall folklore they are called the Watchers. An old inscription found near one of the earliest known Rifts contains only a single warning.

"When the ravens stop watching, run."
the habitants of ravenfall

The Legends

Human myths may be distorted memories of earlier encounters.

Many Legends resemble creatures from human mythology, but centuries of isolation have changed them. Some imitate human voices. Some communicate through light. Some defend specific objects. Some hunt sound. Some become aggressive around bright light — others are drawn to it. Some are enormous; others could sit comfortably on a person's shoulder. Some cannot be seen at all until they move.

Each Legend has its own behaviors, abilities, weaknesses, and story. Understanding those characteristics is essential when humans encounter them — a frightening creature is not necessarily an evil one.

"A frightening creature is not necessarily an evil creature. Understanding what a creature wants can be more important than defeating it."
beyond the veil

The Regions

Explorers have identified five major regions.

If someone calls your name from behind you, do not answer until you know who is speaking.

An enormous forest where paths rearrange themselves when travelers are not looking. Trees grow around abandoned structures from different periods of human history. Something inside the forest has learned how to imitate human voices.

Enormous mechanisms of unknown origin remain embedded underground. Some still move.

A network of caverns, tunnels, mines, and underground ruins. Bioluminescent organisms illuminate portions of the tunnels, while enormous mechanisms of unknown origin remain embedded deep underground. No one knows who built them.

Every empty boat found drifting contains the same thing: a single black feather.

A flooded region of marshes, drowned villages, and dark lakes. Visitors frequently report seeing lights moving beneath the water. Boats have been found drifting completely empty — yet every one contains the same thing: a single black feather.

Forests burned centuries ago that somehow continue to smolder.

A landscape of volcanic stone, abandoned fortresses, and forests burned centuries ago that somehow continue to smolder. Creatures here have adapted to extreme heat and darkness. Ancient structures suggest that someone once attempted to control the Veil from this region.

Every account disagrees on its architecture. All agree on the tower — and the ravens circling it.

Very little is known about it. Maps disagree about its location. People who claim to have visited describe completely different architecture — one described medieval towers, another an industrial city of enormous machines, a third something that hadn't been built yet. Every account agrees on one detail: at the center stands a tower, and thousands of ravens circle it continuously.

the central mystery

The Nameless King

Knowing his name gives him a path into your world.

The weakening Veil is not random. Someone — or something — is deliberately opening the Rifts. According to fragmented stories, an ancient Ravenfall legend once attempted to unite every region of Ravenfall under his control. His true name was deliberately erased from history.

The Legends rebelled against him. The ravens helped seal him somewhere beyond the deepest part of the Veil. For centuries, the prison held. Now the Rifts are opening, ancient mechanisms have begun moving again, creatures are fleeing into the human world, and the ravens are gathering.

Whether he is returning — or whether something worse is happening — remains unknown.

THE PEOPLE BEHIND THE LEGENDS

Storytellers, engineers, and problem-solvers.

Bringing impossible worlds to life requires people working together across very different disciplines. Click any team member to read a short interview.

Cinthia

Founder & CEO

Cinthia founded Odin Kin Entertainment to bring legends to life through imagination, craftsmanship, and immersive experiences. She oversees creative, engineering, and entertainment operations, and believes the best solutions come from understanding the real problem before jumping to an answer.

Q: What do you look for in a new project?

"I want to see that a team understood the real problem before they fell in love with a solution. Listen to the people who'll experience it, challenge your own assumptions, and be willing to improve an idea through iteration — that's how the best Ravenfall experiences got made."

Q: What matters most to you?

"Customer needs, company vision, innovation, collaboration, and outcomes people actually feel. In that order, most days."

ENGINEERING & EXPERIENCE LEADERSHIP

Mae

Co-Director of Engineering & Experiences
Engineering design · Systems thinking · Safety · Physical design · Testing · Guest and performer needs
Q: What's the first thing you check on a new prototype?

"Whether the team actually knows who it's for. A great concept has to be feasible, safe, reliable, and appropriate for the performer wearing it or the guest standing next to it — not just exciting on paper."

Q: What question do you ask most in reviews?

"What happens if this fails while someone's wearing it, or standing next to it, in the middle of a shift?"

AY

Co-Director of Engineering & Experiences
Electronics · Systems · Controls · Technical feasibility · Verification · Reliability · Evidence-based decisions
Q: A team tells you their prototype "just works." What do you say?

"Great — how do you know? Show me the test, the measurement, the log. 'It worked once on my desk' and 'it's reliable' are two very different claims."

Q: What's the most common mistake you see?

"Teams pick a sensor or motor because it's familiar, not because it fits the requirement. Start from what the interaction actually needs to sense or do, then choose the part."

EXPERIENCE DEVELOPMENT

Rayan

Experience Development Engineer
Prototyping · Programming · Interaction · Creative technology · Problem solving · Testing · Iteration
Q: What makes a prop feel "alive" to you?

"When it responds to a person, not just to a button press. Sensors, programmed behaviors, and small interactive effects turn a static object into something that feels like it noticed you're there."

Q: Any advice before a team starts wiring things up?

"Sketch the interaction first — what does the guest do, what does the prop sense, what does it do back — before you touch the Arduino. It saves you from rewiring things twice."

Muskan

Experience Development Engineer
Programming · Interactive systems · Prototyping · Problem solving · Integration · Testing · Iteration
Q: What trips teams up when they combine electronics and fabrication?

"Thinking about inputs, logic, and outputs as separate problems instead of one system. A sensor reading is only useful once you know exactly what the actuator should do with it."

Q: How should a team handle a part failing during a test?

"Expect it. Build in time to fail once, learn why, and try again before showcase day — that's not falling behind, that's the process working."

ODIN KIN // REQUEST FOR PROPOSALS
EXTERNAL CONTRACT OPPORTUNITY

Odin Kin Entertainment — Request for Proposals

Project: Ravenfall Experience Development Initiative
Contract Value: Up to $250,000

Odin Kin Entertainment is seeking an external engineering design contractor to develop the next generation of physical experiences for Feather & Fang.

A MESSAGE FROM ODIN KIN

Something is changing at Feather & Fang. Guests are venturing deeper into Ravenfall, and the experiences waiting beyond the Veil must evolve with them.

Odin Kin's internal teams are currently committed to several major projects. Rather than delay development, the company has opened a competitive contract to outside design teams.

We aren't looking for another decoration. We are looking for something guests will remember.

TWO DEVELOPMENT OPPORTUNITIES

Odin Kin is accepting proposals in two categories.

Immersive Encounter

Develop a compact physical experience capable of transforming an ordinary moment at Feather & Fang into an encounter with Ravenfall. What the guest sees, hears, activates—or believes is watching them—is up to your team.

Creature Experience

Bring one of Ravenfall's habitants into our world through a wearable creature design. We expect to see the vision for the complete creature, even if your prototype focuses on one critical component such as its head, hand, or arm.

We will not tell you exactly what to build. Determining what experience should exist is part of the contract.

FREKI MOONFORGE — BASELINE TECHNICAL EXPECTATIONS

Odin Kin expects physical experiences to sense, respond, or act. At minimum, proposed systems must include a programmable control system, an environmental or user input, and a physical/electronic response. Freki Moonforge will review whether the technology contributes meaningfully to the experience—not simply whether components are present.

SUPPLY CHAIN NOTICE

Contractors may request specialized materials or components during the initial project-development period. Odin Kin will attempt to support reasonable requests; however, procurement cannot guarantee availability or delivery. Strong proposals should include alternatives. A delayed component is an engineering constraint—not a reason for the entire project to stop.

1

Stage 1 — Discovery & Proposal Development

Deadline: Oct 1 & 2 · Early submissions allowed

Odin Kin is intentionally not providing contractors with a detailed product specification. Before proposing a solution, your team must understand the company, the Ravenfall universe, the environment in which the product will operate, and the people who will interact with it.

Do not assume you already know what Odin Kin needs. Investigate. Ask. Then propose.

Confidential Contractor Consultations

Short consultation windows have been reserved with Odin Kin personnel overseeing the contract. Your company will receive approximately 10 minutes with a Director of Engineering & Experiences and 10 minutes with an Experience Development Engineer. These meetings are private. Competing firms will not hear your questions or Odin Kin's responses. Your time is limited. Decide what information matters most before entering the meeting. Odin Kin personnel will answer reasonable questions, but they will not design the product for you.

Executive Consultation

Selected contractor teams will have a short opportunity to speak directly with Cinthia, Founder & CEO of Odin Kin Entertainment. Executive consultation is limited to approximately five minutes. Come prepared. The CEO can clarify Odin Kin's larger priorities and what the company hopes this initiative will accomplish, but she will not select your concept or solve your engineering problems.

What Odin Kin Expects From a Competitive Proposal

We want evidence that your team understands the problem before committing to a product. Show us what you learned from our people. Define the need. Establish requirements. Explore multiple possibilities. Determine how alternatives should be evaluated. Compare them systematically. Consider cost, schedule, users, risks, value creation, ethical implications, and unintended consequences. Then tell us why your proposed direction deserves to move forward.

2

Stage 2 — Design Development

Deadline: Oct 8 & 9

A compelling concept is not enough to win an Odin Kin contract. Freki Moonforge expects contractors to demonstrate that their idea is technically credible. Before significant fabrication begins, Odin Kin expects to understand what you intend to build, how the system works, how its components interact, and what evidence supports your engineering decisions.

Freki Moonforge Technical Review

Your design package should allow another technical team to understand the proposed system without guessing. Show us the geometry. Show us the electrical architecture. Show us the logic. Show us the code. Show us how the pieces communicate. Most importantly, show us the engineering behind your decisions. A polished rendering cannot compensate for a system that has not been engineered.

Creature Design Review

Freki Moonforge understands that developing an entire production-quality creature within the prototype period may not be practical. Contractors may therefore fabricate a critical wearable subsystem. However, Odin Kin must still be able to see the complete creature vision and understand how the engineered subsystem would become part of the final costume.

Experience Design Review

Don't show us only a device sitting on a table. Show us the encounter. Where is the guest? What happens first? What does the system detect? How does it respond? What does the guest perceive? What happens next? If the prototype is scaled, show us what the full installation is intended to become.

3

Stage 3 — Prototype Commission

Deadline: Oct 29 & Oct 30

Your proposal has left the drawing board. Odin Kin now expects proof. Build it. Program it. Break it. Learn why it failed. Fix it. Test it again. The final prototype should demonstrate that the experience you proposed can exist outside a presentation slide.

FINAL CONTRACT REVIEW

Odin Kin is evaluating more than ideas. At final review, your team should arrive with a functional product that could credibly continue toward deployment at Feather & Fang. We expect intentional design, integrated technology, appropriate craftsmanship, repeatable operation, and a clear connection between the final product and the experience originally promised.

PROTOTYPE ENVELOPE

Odin Kin's review facility cannot accommodate full attraction installations. Compact experience prototypes should remain transportable—approximately carry-on size at maximum—and may represent a larger installation at half scale when justified. Wearable prototypes are different: if a performer is supposed to wear it, we need to see it at human scale.

ONE COMPANY. ONE PRIMARY PROPOSAL.

Each contractor team is responsible for delivering one complete primary concept and functional prototype. Odin Kin expects every member of the contractor team to understand how the overall product works, not only the portion they personally developed.

INDIVIDUAL INNOVATION BONUS

Odin Kin notices initiative. Contractor personnel who independently develop an additional functional feature, device, wearable element, or experience component beyond the team's contracted prototype may receive special recognition during final review. Additional work should expand the experience—not simply create another copy of something the team already built.

THE CONTRACT

Odin Kin has authorized a contract of up to $250,000 for the proposal that best demonstrates alignment with the company's needs and a credible path toward implementation. Contractors are competing for more than a single project. Exceptional work may position a firm for future collaboration with Odin Kin Entertainment.

A NOTE FROM ODIN KIN

Our best experiences rarely emerge exactly as they were first imagined. Designs evolve. Requirements change. Prototypes fail. Tests expose problems nobody predicted.

Odin Kin is not looking for a contractor that pretends everything worked the first time. We are looking for a team that knows what to do when it doesn't.

FINAL CONTRACT REVIEW
October 29 — Tue/Thu contractor group
October 30 — Mon/Fri contractor group

Your prototype, engineering evidence, and final proposal will be reviewed as part of Odin Kin's contractor-selection process.

Bring us something worthy of Ravenfall.
